name: Catherine of Siena
knownFor: A Dominican laywoman of Siena whose letters pressed Pope Gregory XI to bring the papacy back from Avignon to Rome. She went to Avignon for Florence in 1376 and later stood by Urban VI in the schism. Her book, the Dialogue, was dictated to her secretaries.
dates: Vida Scudder's chronology of 1905 gives her birth at Siena on 25 March 1347 and her death in Rome on 30 April 1380. Her letter from Avignon is dated 28 June 1376. A Sienese copy of the Dialogue ends in October 1378. John Covel, Master of Christ's College, Cambridge, wrote in 1722 against prayer to the saints. He says Pius II canonized her about eighty years after her death, and gives no year.
place: Siena, where Scudder says she was born in the Strada dell' Oca, near the fountain of Fontebranda. Pisa, in 1375. Avignon, from June to September 1376. Rome, where she lived from 28 November 1378 and died.
tradition: The Latin Papal Church (Avignon to Fifth Lateran)
role: Dominican tertiary, one of the Mantellate; letter writer and peacemaker; author of the Dialogue

keyWorks.title: Letters
keyWorks.about: to popes, cities, rulers and followers, in Vida Scudder's English selection of 1905. Scudder says they were talked rather than written, and dictated to secretaries. Among them are her letters to Gregory XI on his return and the letter of 1376 from Avignon to the Eight of War of Florence.

keyWorks.title: The Dialogue (Libro della divina dottrina)
keyWorks.about: a conversation between God the Father and her soul, dictated to her secretaries. Her secretary Cristofano Guidini gives the title the book was later given, The Book of Divine Doctrine. Algar Thorold put it into English in 1896, and Matilde Fiorilli edited the Italian in 1912.

traces: Stefano Maconi, one of her secretaries, said in the canonization process that he wrote down part of the Dialogue as she dictated it. A note in his own hand, which Matilde Fiorilli quotes, says he put it into Latin. Raymond of Capua writes, in Fiorilli's Italian, that he too was laboring to turn it into Latin.

Edmund Gardner, introducing early English mystical texts in 1910, writes that the Dialogue reached English in 1519 as the Orcharde of Syon, made from Raymond's Latin version, and that Wynkyn de Worde printed an English Life of her from Raymond's Life about 1493.
Fiorilli lists many manuscripts and early printings of the Dialogue in Italian. The printing of 1472 is taken to be the first.

Fiorilli says Stefano Maconi became prior of the Pavia Charterhouse and then general of the Carthusians, and that Tommaso Caffarini of Siena took the largest part in the process for her canonization held at Venice.
remembered: Fiorilli calls Raymond of Capua's Life of her the most authoritative early document about Catherine.
Luciano Banchi, editing the sermons of Bernardino of Siena in 1880, notes that Bernardino was born in the year she died.
Henry Charles Lea, historian of the medieval Inquisition, writes in 1888 that "her constant theme is the corruption of every rank in the hierarchy and the immediate necessity for reform."
A note of 1582 on Teresa of Ávila's manuscript, by the Jesuit Rodrigo Alvarez, names "the books of St. Gertrude, St. Catharine of Siena, or St. Bridget of Sweden" as a measure of true spirit.

uncertain: How far she caused the pope's return. Scudder writes that Gregory, swayed by her representations, returned. Consalvo Duranti, annotating Bridget of Sweden's Revelations in 1628, says Catherine's letters handled the whole matter of the return. Matilde Fiorilli writes that she did much toward it. A notice of Gregory's life in Mansi's collection of church councils names other causes. Gobelinus of Paderborn credits Bridget's revelations. Platina, in his life of Gregory, tells of a bishop's retort that hastened the return. Scudder also writes that Gregory, perhaps regretting his return, became alienated from her.

When the Dialogue was finished. Algar Thorold's title page of 1896 says it was completed in 1370. The Sienese copy Fiorilli prints, and a Florence copy, end in October 1378; a Barberini copy gives 1377. Scudder says it was dictated during 1378. Fiorilli reckons it was written in about three months, from July to October 1378.

The stigmata. Scudder's chronology says she received them at Pisa on 1 April 1375, invisible at her own request. A Bollandist commentary on Christina of Stommeln, in the Acta Sanctorum for June, reports a bull of Sixtus IV that forbade pictures showing her with Christ's wounds, and says it was later softened. The same commentary takes the visible wounds of Lucy of Narni as proof of hers.
Her birth day and her canonization. The day, 25 March 1347, comes from Scudder's chronology alone. The canonization by Pius II rests on John Covel, writing in 1722, who gives no year.
Whether she was summoned to Florence in 1374 to answer charges. Scudder says she was "perhaps" called there to answer charges made by some in her order.
